books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, A. Political Parties and the Rise of the First Two-Party System
A Federalist Debacle and the Era of Good Feelings

stimulus.source_note: Electoral vote totals from the National Archives and Britannica historical election results.
stimulus.text:
| Election | Winner | Electoral votes | Runner-up | Electoral votes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1816 | James Monroe (Democratic-Republican) | 183 | Rufus King (Federalist) | 34 |
| 1820 | James Monroe (Democratic-Republican) | 231 | John Quincy Adams | 1 |

source: original; stimulus is a table of electoral votes from the National Archives
stem: The table best supports calling the years after 1815 the “Era of Good Feelings” because it shows

options.text: one party dominating national politics with almost no opposition
sectional conflict over slavery coming to an end
options.misconception: Sectional conflict over slavery flared in the Missouri crisis of 1819-1820, right in the middle of this era.

options.text: the Federalist Party winning control of Congress
options.misconception: The Federalists were fading, not winning; Monroe's party held the presidency and Congress.

options.text: voting rights expanding to all adult Americans
options.misconception: Voting was still limited in 1820; the expansion of the vote to most white men came later, in the Jacksonian years.

rationales.A: Monroe won 183 electoral votes to 34 in 1816, and 231 to 1 in 1820, when the Federalists barely fielded a candidate. For a time the Democratic-Republicans faced no serious national opposition, which is why the years got their sunny name. Background: the label hides the truth, since the Missouri crisis and Clay's American System showed sectional and economic fights were already growing under the calm.
rationales.B: Sectional conflict over slavery flared in the Missouri crisis of 1819-1820, right in the middle of this era.
rationales.C: The Federalists were fading, not winning. Monroe's party held the presidency and Congress.
rationales.D: Voting was still limited in 1820. The expansion of the vote to most white men came later, in the Jacksonian years.
rationales.general:
1. Read the margins. Monroe wins 183 to 34, then 231 to 1.
2. Ask what a 231-to-1 election means. One party, and almost nobody running against it.
3. Ask what the name claims. Good feelings: a country at peace with itself, politically at least.
4. Put it together. The table is the evidence for the label, and it also warns you the label is too sunny.
Remember: a nickname is a claim, so test it against the numbers underneath it.
